q-115794:
We note that $z=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3z$ and $6z.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3z,6z)=6z.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6z,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2z-1}{6z}=\frac{3z-1}{3z}+\frac{z-1}{6z} \\ 6z\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{6z}) & =6z\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{3z}+\frac{z-1}{6z}) \\ 6z\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{6z}) & =6z\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{3z})+6z\cdot (\frac{z-1}{6z}) \\ \cancel{6z}\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{\cancel{6z}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{3z}\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{\cancel{3z}})+\cancel{6z}\cdot (\frac{z-1}{\cancel{6z}}) \\ 2z-1 & =2\cdot (3z-1)+z-1\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $z,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2z-1 & =2(3z-1)+z-1 \\ 2z-1 & =6z-2+z-1 \\ 2z-1 & =7z-3 \\ 2z-7z & =-3+1 \\ -5z & =-2 \\ z & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $z=0$ as a solution. But since $z=\frac{2}{5}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $z=\frac{2}{5}.$

q-75941:
We note that $m=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3m,5m,$ and $15m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3m,5m,15m)=15m.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $15m,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2m-3}{3m}+\frac{m+5}{5m} & =\frac{m+4}{15m} \\ 15m\cdot (\frac{2m-3}{3m}+\frac{m+5}{5m}) & =15m\cdot (\frac{m+4}{15m}) \\ 15m\cdot (\frac{2m-3}{3m})+15m\cdot (\frac{m+5}{5m}) & =15m\cdot (\frac{m+4}{15m}) \\ 5\cdot 3m\cdot (\frac{2m-3}{3m})+3\cdot 5m\cdot (\frac{m+5}{5m}) & =15m\cdot (\frac{m+4}{15m}) \\ 5\cdot \cancel{3m}\cdot (\frac{2m-3}{\cancel{3m}})+3\cdot \cancel{5m}\cdot (\frac{m+5}{\cancel{5m}}) & =\cancel{15m}\cdot (\frac{m+4}{\cancel{15m}}) \\ 5(2m-3)+3(m+5) & =m+4\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}5(2m-3)+3(m+5) & =m+4 \\ 10m-15+3m+15 & =m+4 \\ 13m & =m+4 \\ 12m & =4 \\ m & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=\frac{1}{3}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=\frac{1}{3}.$

q-116104:
We note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $x$ and ${x}^{2}.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(x,{x}^{2})={x}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${x}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{x})-{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}}) \\ \cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}) & =x\cdot \cancel{x}\cdot (\frac{2}{\cancel{x}})-\cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{x-3}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}) \\ (3x-1) & =x\cdot 2-(x-3) \\ (3x-1) & =2x-(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-1) & =2x-(x-3) \\ 3x-1 & =2x-x+3 \\ 3x-1 & =x+3 \\ 3x-x & =3+1 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. But since $x=2\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $x=2.$

q-69924:
To compute

$$
\frac{5{b}^{2}}{2}÷\frac{b}{7},
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5{b}^{2}}{2}÷\frac{b}{7} & = \\ \frac{5{b}^{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{7}{b} & = \\ \frac{35{b}^{2}}{2b} & = \\ \frac{35{b}^{\cancel{2}}}{2\cancel{b}} & = \\ \frac{35b}{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the final step, we canceled out a common factor of $b$ in the numerator and denominator.

q-288816:
Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0
$$

has the solutions $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ where $a\ne 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.
$$

For the given quadratic equation, we have

$$
a=6,\,b=-17,\,c=-30.
$$

Therefore, the product of the solutions is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{c}{a} & =\frac{(-30)}{6}=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

q-113868:
We want to express the area $A$ between the function $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x+2$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=0$ and $x=3.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x+2$ between the lower limit $x=0$ and the upper limit $x=3,$ as follows:

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}-2x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

q-98716:
We make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(x,\,x+2,\,x(x+2))=x(x+2).
$$

- The values $x=0$ and $x=-2$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{x}-\frac{1}{x+2} & =\frac{4}{x(x+2)} \\ x(x+2)\cdot (\frac{2}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+2}) & =x(x+2)\cdot \frac{4}{x(x+2)} \\ \frac{2x(x+2)}{x}-\frac{x(x+2)}{x+2} & =\frac{4x(x+2)}{x(x+2)} \\ \frac{2\cancel{x}\cdot (x+2)}{\cancel{x}}-\frac{x\cdot \cancel{(x+2)}}{\cancel{x+2}} & =\frac{4\cdot \cancel{x(x+2)}}{\cancel{x(x+2)}} \\ 2(x+2)-x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $x,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x+2)-x & =4 \\ 2x+4-x & =4 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

However, since $x=0$ is not a valid solution, our equation has no solutions.

q-118114:
First, we factor the quadratic denominator, giving us the equation

$$
\frac{4}{d}+\frac{6}{d(d-3)}=\frac{2}{d-3}.
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(d,\,d(d-3),\,d-3)=d(d-3).
$$

- The values $d=0$ and $d=3$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{d}+\frac{6}{d(d-3)} & =\frac{2}{d-3} \\ d(d-3)\cdot (\frac{4}{d}+\frac{6}{d(d-3)}) & =d(d-3)\cdot \frac{2}{d-3} \\ \frac{4d(d-3)}{d}+\frac{6d(d-3)}{d(d-3)} & =\frac{2d(d-3)}{d-3} \\ \frac{4\cdot \cancel{d}\cdot (d-3)}{\cancel{d}}+\frac{6\cdot \cancel{d(d-3)}}{\cancel{d(d-3)}} & =\frac{2d\cdot \cancel{(d-3)}}{\cancel{d-3}} \\ 4(d-3)+6 & =2d\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $d,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(d-3)+6 & =2d \\ 4d-6 & =2d \\ 2d & =6 \\ d & =3\end{aligned}
$$

However, since $d=3$  is not a valid solution, our equation has no solutions.

q-29970:
Since $\frac{2(k+2)}{121y}\cdot Y=\frac{4(k+2)^{2}}{11{y}^{3}},$ we have

$$
Y=\frac{4(k+2)^{2}}{11{y}^{3}}÷\frac{2(k+2)}{121y}.
$$

To compute this quotient, we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4(k+2)^{2}}{11{y}^{3}}÷\frac{2(k+2)}{121y} & = \\ \frac{4(k+2)^{2}}{11{y}^{3}}\cdot \frac{121y}{2(k+2)} & = \\ \frac{2\cdot 2(k+2)\cdot (k+2)}{11y\cdot {y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{11\cdot 11y}{2(k+2)} & = \\ \frac{2\cdot \cancel{2(k+2)}\cdot (k+2)}{\cancel{11y}\cdot {y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{11\cdot \cancel{11y}}{\cancel{2(k+2)}} & = \\ \frac{2(k+2)}{{y}^{2}}\cdot 11 & = \\ \frac{22(k+2)}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-113818:
To compute

$$
\frac{5}{h}÷\frac{10}{k},
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{h}÷\frac{10}{k} & = \\ \frac{5}{h}\cdot \frac{k}{10} & = \\ \frac{5k}{10h} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{5}\cdot k}{\cancel{5}\cdot 2h} & = \\ \frac{k}{2h} & \end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the final step, we canceled out a common factor of $5$ in the numerator and denominator.

q-288819:
Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0
$$

has the solutions $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ where $a\ne 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.
$$

For the given quadratic equation, we have

$$
a=1,\,b=146,\,c=-8\,395.
$$

Therefore, the product of the solutions is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{c}{a} & =\frac{(-8\,395)}{1}=-8\,395.\end{aligned}

q-51135:
Our task is to find $A$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4x+2}{(x+2)(x-1)}=\frac{A}{(x+2)}+\frac{2}{(x-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(x+2)(x-1)$ gives

$$
4x+2=A(x-1)+2(x+2).
$$

For $x=-2$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-2)+2 & =A(-2-1)+2(-2+2) \\ -6 & =-3A \\ A & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-51134:
Our task is to find $B$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+5}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{3}{(x-1)}+\frac{B}{(x+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(x-1)(x+1)$ gives

$$
x+5=3(x+1)+B(x-1).
$$

For $x=-1$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)+5 & =3(-1+1)+B(-1-1) \\ 4 & =-2B \\ B & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-69820:
Our task is to find $A,$ $B$ and $C$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-2{x}^{2}+29x+1}{(4x-1)(x+3)(x+1)} & =\frac{A}{(4x-1)}+\frac{B}{(x+3)}+\frac{C}{(x+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(4x-1)(x+3)(x+1)$ gives

$$
-2{x}^{2}+29x+1=A(x+3)(x+1)+B(4x-1)(x+1)+C(4x-1)(x+3).
$$

For $x=\frac{1}{4}$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}+29(\frac{1}{4})+1 & =A(\frac{1}{4}+3)(\frac{1}{4}+1) \\  & \,+B(4(\frac{1}{4})-1)(\frac{1}{4}+1) \\  & \,+C(4(\frac{1}{4})-1)(\frac{1}{4}+3) \\ -\frac{1}{8}+\frac{29}{4}+1 & =A(\frac{65}{16}) \\ \frac{65}{8} & =A(\frac{65}{16}) \\ A & =\frac{16}{8} \\ A & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-3$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2(-3)^{2}+29(-3)+1 & =A(-3+3)(-3+1) \\  & \,+B(4(-3)-1)(-3+1) \\  & \,+C(4(-3)-1)(-3+3) \\ -18-87+1 & =B(-13)(-2) \\ B & =\frac{-104}{26} \\ B & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-1$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2(-1)^{2}+29(-1)+1 & =A(-1+3)(-1+1) \\  & \,+B(4(-1)-1)(-1+1) \\  & \,+C(4(-1)-1)(-1+3) \\ -2-29+1 & =C(-5)(2) \\ C & =\frac{-30}{-10} \\ C & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{-2{x}^{2}+29x+1}{(4x-1)(x+3)(x+1)}=\frac{2}{(4x-1)}-\frac{4}{(x+3)}+\frac{3}{(x+1)}.
$$

q-10988:
Our task is to find $A,$ $B$ and $C$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13{x}^{2}-19x-16}{(3x+2)(x-3)(x+1)}=\frac{A}{(3x+2)}+\frac{B}{(x-3)}+\frac{C}{(x+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(3x+2)(x-3)(x+1)$ gives

$$
13{x}^{2}-19x-16=A(x-3)(x+1)+B(3x+2)(x+1)+C(3x+2)(x-3).
$$

For $x=-\frac{2}{3}$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}13{(-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-19(-\frac{2}{3})-16 & =A(-\frac{2}{3}-3)(-\frac{2}{3}+1) \\  & \,+B(3(-\frac{2}{3})+2)(-\frac{2}{3}+1) \\  & \,+C(3(-\frac{2}{3})+1)(-\frac{2}{3}-3) \\ \frac{52}{9}+\frac{38}{3}-16 & =A(\frac{(-11)(1)}{9}) \\ \frac{52+114-144}{9} & =A(-\frac{11}{9}) \\ A & =-\frac{22}{11} \\ A & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=3$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}13(3)^{2}-19(3)-16 & =A(3-3)(3+1) \\  & \,+B(3(3)+2)(3+1) \\  & \,+C(3(3)+2)(3-3) \\ 117-57-16 & =B(44) \\ B & =\frac{44}{44} \\ B & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-1$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}13(-1)^{2}-19(-1)-16 & =A(-1-3)(-1+1) \\  & \,+B(3(-1)+2)(-1+1) \\  & \,+C(3(-1)+2)(-1-3) \\ 13+19-16 & =C(4) \\ C & =\frac{16}{4} \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B+C & =(-2)+1+4=3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-288406:
Since the equation is true for all values of $x,$ the expressions on both sides must be exactly the same. That means the coefficients of the matching powers of $x$ must be equal.

We compare the linear terms on both sides. On the left-hand side, the coefficient of $x$ is $m.$ On the right-hand side, the coefficient of $x$ is $-3.$

So, we have

$$
m=-3.
$$
